solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Circulates counterfeit US money, but shifts responsibility (6,3,4)

blocks.note: a buck is an American dollar; a forger puts fake ones into circulation
an idiom for handing blame on to someone else

annotation.surface: A forger spreading fake dollars tries to pin the blame elsewhere.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half takes the idiom literally: passing a dud buck, a counterfeit dollar, is the forger's crime, so both halves land on the same phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to pass the buck is to push a duty or the blame on to someone else, from the marker once passed round a poker table.

entries.clue: In the midst of anxiety, a case for doctor (7)

indicatorNotes.a case for: anxiety serves as a case, a casing, wrapped round the doctor

blocks.note: angst = anxiety, a word borrowed from German
MO = Medical Officer, an army doctor

annotation.surface: A worried patient seems to be making the case for seeing a doctor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A case for doctor' reads as 'a matter for the doctor'; the anxiety word is the case, opened after its first letter to take the doctor in.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a preposition meaning surrounded by or in the middle of a group.

entries.clue: Asian to look for, by the sound of it (4)

indicatorNotes.by the sound of it: tells you to take the word as heard, not as spelt

blocks.note: seek = look for; the answer is spelt differently but said the same

annotation.walkthrough: A Sikh follows Sikhism, a religion from the Punjab in India, so 'Asian' is a fair if broad definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: Sikhism began in the Punjab, so its followers are typically South Asian.

entries.clue: Deduces it is wrong to be led astray (7)

indicatorNotes.it is wrong: the letters of the word before it are wrongly ordered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A moralist concludes that being tempted into sin is wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is a single word, which the surface hides by making 'Deduces' the main verb of a moral judgment.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to be seduced is to be tempted away from the right path, especially into sin.

entries.clue: Pet’s held in arms — the stray (7)

indicatorNotes.stray: letters that stray wander out of their order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: Someone cradles a stray animal they have taken in as a pet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Held in' looks like it wants the answer hidden or contained, but here it only links the pet to its letters; 'stray' does the work.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the small caged rodent is one of the commonest children's pets.

entries.clue: Run away from a flash of lightning (4)

blocks.note: to run off suddenly, as a startled horse does
a single streak of lightning, the thunder-god's missile

annotation.surface: Someone flees in fright from a lightning strike.
annotation.walkthrough: 'From' makes the surface a cause and effect, fleeing because of the lightning; it only joins two separate meanings of one word.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses share sudden speed: a horse that bolts shoots off, and a bolt of lightning is one sudden streak.

entries.clue: One needs a regular supply of drugs to keep going (7)

annotation.definition: One needs a regular supply of drugs to keep going

blocks.clueFragment: One needs a regular supply of drugs
blocks.note: reads as an addict's craving; it is a shop's need for steady deliveries of medicines
reads as getting through the day; it means staying in business

annotation.surface: It sounds like a description of an addict.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as dependency; the one who needs the drugs to keep going is the shop that sells them. A chemist is the British word for a pharmacy or pharmacist.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: a chemist's shop cannot trade without a steady restocking of medicines.

entries.clue: Soldiers may see it as a moving religious ceremony (6,7)

blocks.note: troops sent into real operations, rather than training, are said to see this
a church ceremony taken literally as one that is lively and on the move

annotation.surface: Troops are stirred by a church parade.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Moving' wants to mean emotionally touching; the second half takes it literally, a church service full of activity.
annotation.definitionFit: A fixed military phrase for deployment in operations, then read literally as a lively church service.

entries.clue: No doubt one’s aware of the pressure we’re under (13)

annotation.definition: No doubt one’s aware of the pressure we’re under

blocks.note: reads as a sympathetic friend; it is a professional whose job is to know
reads as stress; it is the air pressure over our heads, the highs and lows

annotation.surface: A sympathetic friend who understands how stressed we all are.
annotation.walkthrough: The pressure sounds like stress; it is atmospheric pressure, which sits over everyone and which a weather scientist measures.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: a weather scientist tracks barometric pressure, the weight of air we all live under.

entries.clue: Hit century, made fast (7)

blocks.note: C = 100, the Roman numeral
made fast = secured, locked

annotation.surface: A cricketer smashes a hundred at speed.
annotation.walkthrough: The cricket picture makes 'fast' mean quick; here it means secure. To clock someone is British slang for hitting them.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal British usage: to clock someone is to punch them, especially on the face or head.

entries.clue: Man taking in some tennis, returning kind of cross (7)

indicatorNotes.taking in: the man takes the next piece inside him
indicatorNotes.returning: the piece comes back the other way

blocks.note: a man is a male
a set is one portion of a tennis match

annotation.surface: A player gets grumpy on coming back from a spell of tennis.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' sits at the end looking like 'angry'; with 'kind of' it is the eight-pointed cross of the Knights of Malta.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the Maltese cross, with four arrowhead arms, is one named kind of cross.

entries.clue: Order a gin for Swedish girl? (4)

indicatorNotes.Order: put the letters into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 4 letters

annotation.surface: Someone buys a drink at the bar for a Scandinavian woman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Order' reads as asking the barman; it is the instruction to reorder. The question mark marks the definition as one example of a Swedish name.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Inga is a typical Scandinavian girl's name.

entries.clue: A charming French accent (5)

blocks.note: taken as it stands
cute = charming

annotation.surface: Someone finds a French way of speaking attractive.
annotation.walkthrough: 'French accent' reads as a way of speaking; it is the written mark over the e in café.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the acute is one of the diacritic marks used in French spelling.

entries.clue: Sneer? I beg to differ! (4)

indicatorNotes.to differ: the letters take a different arrangement

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 4 letters

annotation.surface: A polite disagreement answering a jibe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I beg to differ' is a set phrase for polite disagreement, which disguises the split into fodder and instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a gibe is a taunting, mocking remark, much like a sneer.

entries.clue: Tour arranged around mid-April somewhere in Cornwall (5)

indicatorNotes.arranged: the letters are put in a new arrangement
indicatorNotes.around: the rearranged letters go round the next piece
indicatorNotes.mid-: take the middle of the word

blocks.note: anagram fodder, rearranged to TURO
R is the middle letter of APRIL

annotation.surface: A holiday itinerary includes a spring stop in the West Country.
annotation.walkthrough: Cornwall is the far south-western county of England, and the answer is its cathedral city.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Truro is Cornwall's only city, one place in the county.

entries.clue: They work around the clock (5)

blocks.note: reads as people who labour, workers on a farm or ship
reads as nonstop; it means literally travelling round a clock face

annotation.surface: Shift workers putting in 24-hour days.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Around the clock' means nonstop, and workers are often called hands; the literal reading is the pointers going round a clock face.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses at once: hands are farm or factory workers and the pointers that sweep a clock's face.

entries.clue: Appeared to act? (7)

blocks.note: reads as seemed; it means came into view on stage
reads as pretending; it is an actor coming on to perform

annotation.walkthrough: 'Appeared to act' reads as 'seemed to be pretending'; it means came on stage to perform, which in a script's directions is the one-word cue for an arrival.
annotation.definitionFit: A theatrical sense: an actor who comes on stage has appeared in order to act, as a script's stage directions say.

entries.clue: Minister provides framework for a nuclear establishment (7)

indicatorNotes.provides framework for: the minister forms a frame round the next piece

blocks.note: a rector is a parish priest, a minister of religion
taken as it stands

annotation.surface: A government minister sets out a policy for a nuclear plant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Minister' pulls towards government; it is a church minister, a parish priest.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose sense: the reactor is the installation at the heart of a nuclear plant, where the chain reaction runs.

entries.clue: Eastern politician, Queen or ruler (7)

blocks.note: E = east
MP = Member of Parliament
ER = Elizabeth Regina
taken as it stands

annotation.surface: A list of Asian authorities: statesman, queen or king.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a link offering a choice between Queen and ruler; it is a piece of the answer, and only 'ruler' defines.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: an emperor is the highest kind of ruler, sovereign of an empire.

entries.clue: Happy and relaxed after record rise (7)

indicatorNotes.rise: in a down answer, a piece that rises reads upwards, bottom to top
indicatorNotes.after: the relaxed piece comes after the record piece

blocks.note: LP = long-playing record
eased = relaxed

annotation.surface: Someone is delighted after a record-breaking pay rise.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Record rise' reads as an all-time high; it is the vinyl record turned upside down in this down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: pleased means happy or satisfied.

entries.clue: Object when going into rent is investment (7)

indicatorNotes.when going into: the object goes inside the next piece

blocks.note: an aim is an object, a goal
taken as it stands

annotation.surface: Someone protests about putting their rent money into an investment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Investment' looks financial; it means clothing, from invest in its old sense of dressing someone in robes, so the definition is fair if old-fashioned.
annotation.definitionFit: An old sense: to invest once meant to clothe, so an investment is a garment, and raiment is clothing.

entries.clue: Fear led to riot concerning central government (7)

indicatorNotes.riot: letters running riot are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: Public fear turned into unrest against the state.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Riot' sits naturally after 'led to', so the surface reads as fear causing a riot; 'Fear led' is the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain sense: federal describes the central government of a union of states, as opposed to the states themselves.

entries.clue: FA’s receiving nets to mount ties (7)

indicatorNotes.receiving: the first piece takes the next piece inside it
indicatorNotes.to mount: in a down answer, climbing up means reading from the bottom

blocks.note: taken as it stands
taken as it stands, then turned upwards

annotation.surface: The Football Association is getting goal nets set up for its fixtures.
annotation.walkthrough: The FA is England's Football Association, and 'ties' look like its cup matches; here ties is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to tie something is to fasten it, both verbs meaning secure.

entries.clue: Sinner I reformed pulls up, perhaps (5,2)

indicatorNotes.reformed: the letters are formed again in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A reformed sinner confesses that they still slip up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pulls up' is what a rider does to a horse; 'perhaps' warns that the answer is one way of pulling up.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a rider pulls up a horse by tightening the reins, one way of stopping.

entries.clue: Look in half a dozen directions (4)

blocks.note: VI = 6 in Roman numerals
E and W, east and west, two compass directions

annotation.surface: Someone glances around in six different directions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as placing the look inside the directions; it is only a link, and the pieces simply follow one another.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to view something is to look at it.

entries.clue: Placing of the winner may create rifts (5)

indicatorNotes.may create: the answer's letters, rearranged, create the word that follows

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters

annotation.surface: Awarding the top prize could cause splits in the team.
annotation.walkthrough: This runs backwards from the usual order: the answer is what gets rearranged, and the word at the end is what it creates.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain sense: the winner of a race is placed first.

entries.clue: It may be used to lift a football side (4)

annotation.definition: It may be used to lift

blocks.clueFragment: It may be used to lift
blocks.note: the aerofoil that gives an aircraft or bird its lift
the flank of a football pitch, or the player who works it

annotation.surface: A tool for hoisting a football team's morale.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lift a football side' reads as raising a team's spirits; the two halves split apart as flight and a flank of the pitch.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: an aerofoil produces lift for a plane or bird, and the flanks of a football pitch share the name.

entries.clue: It may be sucked or blown (4)

annotation.definition: It may be sucked or blown

blocks.note: something a smoker draws on
something a musician plays by blowing into it

annotation.walkthrough: One word covers both actions: smokers draw on a tobacco pipe, and pipers blow into a musical one.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses at once: a tobacco pipe is smoked by sucking, and a musical pipe is played by blowing.

entries.clue: Rogue quietly abandoned swindle (4)

indicatorNotes.abandoned: the piece before it is dropped

blocks.note: a scamp is a rogue
p = piano, quietly in music; this is the letter removed

annotation.surface: A crook who has quietly walked out on a con.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'quietly abandoned' sound like slipping away; it tells you to drop the musical soft letter from the rogue.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a scam is a dishonest scheme to cheat someone out of money.

entries.clue: I keep going round part of Spain (7)

indicatorNotes.going round: the keep goes round the I

blocks.note: a keep is the main tower of a castle, and stands for it
taken as it stands

annotation.surface: A traveller keeps touring a region of Spain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I keep going' reads as a phrase about carrying on; 'keep' is a noun, the stronghold, which goes round the I.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Castile is a historic region and former kingdom of central Spain.

entries.clue: Pardons and releases (7)

blocks.note: forgives a fault
lets someone off a duty

annotation.surface: An authority granting pardons and freeing prisoners.
annotation.walkthrough: Both senses are everyday: excusing a fault forgives it, and excusing someone from school or a duty lets them off.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses of one verb: to forgive a lapse, and to free someone from an obligation.

entries.clue: Could be a circular plug (13)

blocks.note: reads as round in shape; a circular is a leaflet sent round to many
reads as a bung; it is a piece of promotion

annotation.surface: It sounds like a round stopper for a sink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Circular plug' pictures a round bung; a circular is a flyer delivered to many homes, and to plug something is to promote it.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: a flyer sent round to promote a product is one form of publicity notice.
